summary.big_idea: Use the key chemistry ideas and methods from revision and exam practice accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exam_questions.statement:
A student is investigating how the concentration of a reactant affects the rate of a reaction. Potassium iodate reacts with a reducing agent to produce iodine; the reaction is followed with starch solution as an indicator, which turns blue-black when iodine is present. The method: 10 cm$^3$ potassium iodate solution is placed into a conical flask; 5 cm$^3$ starch solution is added; the timer is started as 5 cm$^3$ of the reducing agent is added; the timer is stopped when the mixture goes blue-black; the time taken (to the nearest second) is recorded. The experiment is repeated four times, varying the volumes of potassium iodate solution and water, as in Table 1.1 (volume potassium iodate/cm$^3$, volume water/cm$^3$, time/s, $1/\text{time}$): (10, 0, 10, 0.100); (8, 2, 13, 0.077); (6, 4, ?, ?); (4, 6, 30, 0.033); (2, 8, ?, ?). Figure 1.1 shows two stopclocks: for the 6 cm$^3$ potassium iodate experiment the stopclock reads 0:17.3; for the 2 cm$^3$ potassium iodate experiment it reads 1:05.0.
(a) Read the stopclocks and record the times (to the nearest second) for the 6 cm$^3$ and 2 cm$^3$ experiments in Table 1.1. [2]
(b)(i) Calculate $1/\text{time}$ (rate) for the missing values and enter the results in the last column of Table 1.1. [1]
(ii) Plot a graph of $1/\text{time}$ (vertical axis) against the volume of potassium iodate solution/cm$^3$, drawing the best straight line through the origin. [4]
(c)(i) State what your graph tells you about how the rate of the reaction depends upon the volume of potassium iodate solution present. [1]
(ii) When the potassium iodate is reduced, iodine is formed. What observation made by the student confirms this? [1]
(iii) Why are different volumes of water used in each experiment? [1]
exam_questions.answer:
(a) 6 cm$^3$ experiment: time = 17 s; 2 cm$^3$ experiment: time = 65 s.
(b)(i) For 6 cm$^3$: $1/17 = 0.059$ (to 3 d.p.); for 2 cm$^3$: $1/65 = 0.015$ (to 3 d.p.).
(ii) A straight line of best fit passing through the origin, rising left to right (rate increases steadily as volume of potassium iodate increases).
(c)(i) The rate is directly proportional to the volume (hence concentration) of potassium iodate solution used — doubling the volume of potassium iodate roughly doubles the rate (1/time).
(ii) The mixture turning/going blue-black (the starch–iodine complex forming) confirms iodine has been produced.
(iii) The volume of water is varied so that the total volume of liquid in the flask is kept constant in every experiment — this means only the concentration of potassium iodate is being changed, keeping it the only variable affecting the rate (a fair test).
exam_questions.full_solution:
The stopclock under the 6 cm$^3$ label reads '0:17.3' (17.3 s) and the one under the 2 cm$^3$ label reads '1:05.0' (1 minute 5.0 seconds = 65.0 s). Rounded to the nearest second these are 17 s and 65 s, which slot into the time column of Table 1.1.

Rate is defined here as $1/\text{time}$. Checking the given entries shows the 3-decimal-place convention ($1/10=0.100$, $1/13=0.0769\approx0.077$, $1/30=0.0333\approx0.033$), so: $1/17 = 0.05882\ldots \approx 0.059$ and $1/65 = 0.01538\ldots \approx 0.015$.

Plotting $1/\text{time}$ (y-axis) against volume of potassium iodate (x-axis) using the five pairs (10, 0.100), (8, 0.077), (6, 0.059), (4, 0.033), (2, 0.015): the points lie close to a straight line through the origin (gradient about 0.010 per cm$^3$), so a single ruled best-fit line through the origin is drawn.

The straight line through the origin shows that the rate is directly proportional to the volume, and hence the concentration, of potassium iodate: more concentrated potassium iodate → shorter time → larger 1/time → faster rate. The constant total volume (10 cm$^3$ potassium iodate + water, 5 cm$^3$ starch and 5 cm$^3$ reducing agent each time) is why the water volume is varied: it is the standard way of changing only the concentration of one reagent while keeping everything else (total volume, and so the concentrations of starch and reducing agent) constant, making it a fair test.
mark_scheme: B1 for time = 17 (s) for the 6 cm3 experiment
B1 for time = 65 (s) for the 2 cm3 experiment
B1 for both 1/time values correct: 0.059 (6 cm3) and 0.015 (2 cm3), consistent with 3 d.p. given in table
M1 for plotting all 5 points correctly
M1 for a single straight best-fit line (not point-to-point)
M1 for line passing through (or very close to) the origin
M1 for line being a reasonable 'best fit' through the scatter of points
B1 for stating rate is (directly) proportional to volume/concentration of potassium iodate
B1 for the mixture turning/going blue-black
B1 for idea that water keeps total volume (hence other concentrations) constant / fair test

exam_questions.statement:
The science class is making a display to show the elements in Period 3 of the Periodic Table (Figure 2.1): Na (11), Mg (12), Al (13), Si (14), P (15), S (16), Cl (17), Ar (18). Sodium (11) and phosphorus (15) are each shown in a bottle covered with a liquid (to stop the element reacting with air); one is covered with water, the other with oil. Figure 2.2 shows a student burning a sample of element 16 (sulfur) in a Bunsen flame and then holding it in a gas-jar of oxygen; after burning, the student adds water to the gas-jar, puts on the lid, shakes it, then adds Universal Indicator (full-range indicator) solution.
(a) Write the names of element number 12 and element number 14. [2]
(b) Elements 11 and 15 are contained in bottles and covered with a liquid to prevent the element reacting with air. Complete: the element covered by water is ____; the element covered by oil is ____. [1]
(c) The gas-jars holding samples of elements 17 and 18 have lost their labels. How can a student tell from the appearance of the gases which gas-jar contains element number 17? [1]
(d) Describe an experiment that a student can do to show that element number 13 is a metal, and state the observation the student will make. [2]
(e)(i) State the flame colour of the burning element number 16. [1]
(ii) Suggest why the student adds water to the gas-jar. [1]
(iii) State the colour of the Universal Indicator in the gas-jar. [1]
(iv) The student does the same experiment with a piece of element number 12. Suggest the colour of the Universal Indicator in this gas-jar. [1]
exam_questions.answer:
(a) Element 12 = magnesium; element 14 = silicon.
(b) Covered by water = phosphorus (element 15); covered by oil = sodium (element 11).
(c) Element 17 is chlorine, a pale green/yellow-green gas; element 18 is argon, a colourless gas — the coloured gas-jar is chlorine, the colourless one is argon.
(d) e.g. Connect the piece of element 13 (aluminium) into a simple circuit with a battery/cell and a bulb (lamp) using wires with crocodile clips; the observation is that the bulb lights up, showing the element conducts electricity (a property of metals). (Alternative valid answers: show it is malleable by hitting it with a hammer — it bends/flattens without shattering; or show it conducts heat.)
(e)(i) Blue (sulfur burns with a blue flame).
(ii) Water is added so the sulfur dioxide gas (SO$_2$) produced dissolves in it, forming an acidic solution whose pH can then be tested with the indicator.
(iii) Red/orange (showing the solution is acidic, since SO$_2$ dissolves to form sulfurous/sulfuric acid).
(iv) Blue/purple (magnesium forms magnesium oxide, a basic oxide, which reacts with water to give a mildly alkaline solution).
exam_questions.full_solution:
Period 3 runs Na(11)–Ar(18), so element 12 is magnesium and element 14 is silicon, read directly off the diagram.

Of elements 11 (Na) and 15 (P), sodium is a very reactive metal that reacts vigorously with both air and water, so it is stored under oil (unreactive towards it); (white) phosphorus is so reactive with oxygen in air that it spontaneously ignites, so it is stored under water instead (it does not react with water). So water → phosphorus, oil → sodium.

Element 17 is chlorine, Cl$_2$, which is a pale green/yellow-green coloured gas; element 18 is argon, a noble gas which is colourless. A student can simply look at the two gas-jars: the one with a visible green-yellow tinge is chlorine (element 17), the colourless one is argon.

Element 13 is aluminium. To show it is a metal, the simplest distinguishing test used at this level is electrical conductivity: metals (giant metallic lattices with delocalised electrons) conduct electricity when solid, non-metals generally do not. Connecting the aluminium into a circuit with a cell and a bulb and seeing the bulb light up demonstrates conduction.

Element 16 is sulfur. Burning sulfur in oxygen gives a blue flame and produces sulfur dioxide gas: S + O$_2$ → SO$_2$. Water is added afterwards so the SO$_2$ gas dissolves, giving a solution of sulfurous acid (and some further oxidation/dissolving gives sulfuric acid); testing with Universal Indicator then shows a red/orange colour, confirming the solution is acidic — consistent with the general rule that oxides of non-metals are acidic (or neutral). Element 12 is magnesium; burning magnesium in oxygen gives magnesium oxide (2Mg + O$_2$ → 2MgO), a metal oxide, which is basic: dissolved/suspended in water it gives a weakly alkaline solution (magnesium hydroxide is only sparingly soluble, so the solution is only mildly alkaline), turning Universal Indicator blue/purple — consistent with the general rule that oxides of metals are basic.
mark_scheme: B1 element 12 = magnesium
B1 element 14 = silicon
B1 water = phosphorus AND oil = sodium (both needed for the mark)
B1 chlorine (17) is green/yellow-green coloured, argon (18) is colourless — correct identification by colour
M1 valid method described (e.g. test electrical conductivity in a circuit with cell and bulb)
A1 correct observation stated (bulb lights up / conducts electricity, or equivalent for malleability test)
B1 blue flame
B1 water dissolves the sulfur dioxide gas so its acidity can be tested
B1 red/orange (acidic)
B1 blue/purple (alkaline, since MgO is a basic oxide)

exam_questions.statement:
(a) Water is a compound which contains the elements hydrogen and oxygen. Describe one difference, other than physical state, between the compound water and a mixture of the elements hydrogen and oxygen. [2]
(b) Table 4.1 gives melting point, boiling point and solubility in water for water and three compounds: sodium chloride (m.p. 801 °C, b.p. 1413 °C, soluble), silicon dioxide (m.p. 1650 °C, b.p. 2230 °C, insoluble), hexane (m.p. −95 °C, b.p. 69 °C, insoluble).
(i) State which compound in Table 4.1 could be separated from a mixture with water by filtration. [1]
(ii) Explain why the other two compounds cannot be separated from a mixture with water by filtration. [2]
(iii) A student viewed sodium chloride crystals under a microscope and saw small cube-shaped crystals (Figure 4.1). Draw a simple diagram of the structure of sodium chloride, clearly showing the nature and arrangement of the particles involved, and explaining why the crystals have the cube shape shown. [3]
(c) The student is asked to use the reaction between the insoluble compound copper carbonate and dilute sulfuric acid to make some crystals of copper sulfate. Describe the main steps of a method the student should use. [4]
exam_questions.answer:
(a) A compound is a pure substance with a fixed/definite composition and has chemical/physical properties completely different from those of its constituent elements, formed by a chemical reaction that cannot be reversed by physical means — e.g. water does not burn and does not support combustion, unlike the separate gases hydrogen (flammable) and oxygen (supports combustion); a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen retains the properties of each gas and can be present in any ratio, and the gases can be separated again by physical means, whereas the hydrogen and oxygen in water are chemically bonded and can only be separated by a chemical process such as electrolysis.
(b)(i) Silicon dioxide (it is an insoluble solid).
(ii) Sodium chloride is soluble, so it dissolves/forms a solution with water and passes straight through the filter paper (no solid residue is left to be trapped). Hexane is insoluble but is a liquid (immiscible with water, forming a separate layer); filtration only separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, not two liquids, so hexane would need a separating funnel, not filtration.
(iii) Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice: a regular, repeating 3-D arrangement of alternating positive sodium ions (Na$^+$) and negative chloride ions (Cl$^-$), held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between the oppositely charged ions acting in all directions. Because this ionic arrangement repeats in a fixed, regular cubic pattern at the atomic/ionic scale, the whole visible crystal also grows into a cube shape.
(c) Add excess (powdered) copper carbonate to a measured volume of dilute sulfuric acid in a beaker and stir until no more dissolves (effervescence stops, showing all the acid has reacted and copper carbonate is in excess). Filter the mixture to remove the unreacted excess copper carbonate, keeping the blue filtrate (copper sulfate solution). Gently heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to evaporate off some of the water until it is saturated (tested by dipping in a cold glass rod and checking crystals form on it). Leave the hot saturated solution to cool slowly so that crystals of (hydrated) copper sulfate form; filter off the crystals, wash them with a little cold water, and dry them (e.g. between sheets of filter paper).
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) The key chemical distinction between a compound and a mixture of its elements is that a compound's atoms are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio and the compound has new properties unlike either starting element (e.g. water is a liquid that extinguishes fires, while H$_2$ gas is explosive/flammable and O$_2$ supports burning); a mixture is just elements physically together, each retaining its own properties, in any proportion, separable again by physical means (e.g. diffusion/different boiling points), unlike a compound which requires a chemical reaction (e.g. electrolysis of water) to split it back into its elements.

(b) Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid by trapping solid particles too large to pass through the filter paper's pores while the liquid (filtrate) passes through. Of the three compounds: sodium chloride is soluble, so no solid residue exists to be caught by the paper — it just dissolves into the filtrate. Silicon dioxide is an insoluble solid, so it is exactly what filtration is designed to remove: it stays behind as a residue. Hexane is insoluble but it is a liquid, forming a separate (oily) layer rather than solid particles; filtration cannot separate two immiscible liquids — that requires a separating funnel, exploiting the difference in density between the two liquid layers.

For the structure of sodium chloride (iii): NaCl is a giant ionic lattice, with Na$^+$ and Cl$^-$ ions alternating in a regular 3-D grid, each ion surrounded by six oppositely charged neighbours (6:6 co-ordination), held by strong electrostatic (ionic) attraction extending through the whole crystal in every direction. This underlying cubic symmetry of the lattice is the reason the macroscopic crystals grow as small cubes — the regular repeating unit cell itself is cubic, so cleavage and growth naturally produce cube-shaped crystals, exactly as seen under the microscope in Figure 4.1.

(c) This is the standard 'insoluble base/carbonate + acid → soluble salt' preparation. Copper carbonate (CuCO$_3$, insoluble, green-blue solid) is added in excess to dilute sulfuric acid: CuCO$_3$(s) + H$_2$SO$_4$(aq) → CuSO$_4$(aq) + H$_2$O(l) + CO$_2$(g). Using excess solid ensures all the acid is used up (no acid impurity remains in the product), shown by effervescence (CO$_2$ bubbles) stopping. Filtering removes the leftover unreacted solid copper carbonate, leaving a pure blue solution of copper sulfate. This solution is then concentrated by gentle heating/evaporation until saturated, and allowed to cool slowly, which lets regular hydrated copper sulfate crystals (CuSO$_4$·5H$_2$O) grow out of solution (slow cooling favours larger, well-formed crystals). Finally the crystals are filtered off from the remaining liquid and dried without excessive heating, to avoid driving off the water of crystallisation.
mark_scheme: M1 compound has fixed composition / new properties unlike its elements, with example (e.g. water does not burn, unlike H2/O2)
A1 mixture retains properties of each element / can be in any ratio / separated by physical means (compound only by chemical means)
B1 silicon dioxide
M1 sodium chloride is soluble so dissolves/passes through filter paper
A1 hexane is an insoluble liquid, not a solid — filtration only separates insoluble solid from liquid (needs separating funnel instead)
B1 regular/repeating giant lattice of alternating Na+ and Cl- ions shown clearly
B1 held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions
B1 explanation that the regular cubic arrangement of ions causes the cube-shaped crystal
M1 excess copper carbonate added to dilute sulfuric acid (react until no more fizzing/dissolving)
M1 filter to remove excess unreacted copper carbonate
M1 heat/evaporate filtrate to saturation point
A1 cool (slowly) to crystallise, then filter and dry the crystals

exam_questions.statement:
Figure 5.1 shows apparatus (thermometer, insulated beaker) a student used to investigate temperature changes during chemical reactions, starting each time from 22 °C. Table 5.1: Experiment 1: dilute hydrochloric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate, final temperature 16 °C. Experiment 2: dilute hydrochloric acid + potassium hydroxide solution, final temperature 26 °C. Experiment 3: magnesium + copper sulfate solution, final temperature 43 °C. Experiment 4: copper + magnesium sulfate solution, final temperature 22 °C.
(a)(i) Explain which experiment (1, 2, 3 or 4) was a reaction involving an alkali. [1]
(ii) State and explain which experiment was an endothermic reaction. [1]
(iii) Suggest and explain a reason for the result obtained in experiment 4. [2]
(b) The student carried out two further experiments (5 and 6) on the reaction between zinc and copper sulfate solution: in experiment 5 she used 3.25 g of zinc powder, in experiment 6 a single piece of zinc also of mass 3.25 g. She observed the thermometer readings over five minutes in each. Predict and explain any difference in how the temperature would change between experiments 5 and 6. [3]
(c) In the reaction in (b), zinc atoms react with copper ions: Zn(s) + Cu$^{2+}$(aq) → Zn$^{2+}$(aq) + Cu(s). Explain, in terms of the transfer of electrons, why this reaction is an example of oxidation and reduction (redox). [1]
exam_questions.answer:
(a)(i) Experiment 2 — potassium hydroxide solution is a true alkali (a soluble metal hydroxide that releases OH$^-$ ions in solution); sodium hydrogencarbonate is a salt, not classed as an alkali.
(ii) Experiment 1 — the final temperature (16 °C) is lower than the starting temperature (22 °C), showing the reaction absorbed heat energy from the surroundings, i.e. it is endothermic.
(iii) No temperature change occurred (22 °C throughout) because no reaction took place: copper is less reactive than magnesium, so copper metal cannot displace magnesium from magnesium sulfate solution (reactivity series).
(b) The temperature would rise faster (more steeply, reaching its maximum sooner) in experiment 5 than in experiment 6, because the zinc powder has a much greater surface area in contact with the copper sulfate solution than the single piece of the same mass, so there are more collisions between zinc atoms and copper ions per second, giving a faster rate of reaction and so a faster rate of heat release. If both reactions went to completion the same total energy would be released, but in the five minutes the single piece may not have finished reacting, and it loses heat to the surroundings while it reacts slowly, so experiment 6 is likely to reach a lower maximum temperature in that time.
(c) Zn atoms lose electrons to form Zn$^{2+}$ ions (oxidation = loss of electrons), while Cu$^{2+}$ ions gain electrons to form Cu atoms (reduction = gain of electrons); because both processes happen together (electrons are transferred directly from Zn to Cu$^{2+}$), the reaction is a redox reaction.
exam_questions.full_solution:
An alkali, strictly, is a soluble base that releases hydroxide ions (OH$^-$) in aqueous solution — potassium hydroxide solution (experiment 2) fits this exactly. Sodium hydrogencarbonate is a salt (weakly basic in solution but not classified as 'an alkali' at this level), so experiment 1 is excluded from that category.

Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings, so the surroundings (and the reaction mixture itself) cool down — exactly what is observed in experiment 1, where the temperature fell from 22 °C to 16 °C. (By contrast experiments 2 and 3, where temperature rose, are exothermic.)

Experiment 4 pairs copper metal with magnesium sulfate solution. In the reactivity series, magnesium is well above copper, so copper cannot displace magnesium from its salt solution (only a more reactive metal can displace a less reactive one from its compound). With no reaction occurring, there is no energy released or absorbed, so the temperature simply stays at the starting value of 22 °C.

For zinc powder vs a single lump of the same mass reacting with copper sulfate solution: surface area is the key variable. Powdered zinc presents a much larger total surface area exposed to the solution, so many more zinc atoms are simultaneously available to collide with and react with Cu$^{2+}$ ions — this speeds up the rate of reaction and therefore the rate of heat release, so the temperature in experiment 5 rises more steeply and reaches its peak sooner. If both reactions were allowed to go to completion, the same mass (and so the same number of moles) of zinc would release the same total energy. However, the readings are taken for only five minutes: the single piece reacts slowly, may not have finished reacting in that time, and loses more heat to the surroundings while it reacts, so its temperature rises more gradually and probably reaches a lower maximum within the five minutes.

For the redox explanation: in Zn(s) + Cu$^{2+}$(aq) → Zn$^{2+}$(aq) + Cu(s), each Zn atom loses 2 electrons to become Zn$^{2+}$ (this loss of electrons is, by definition, oxidation), while each Cu$^{2+}$ ion gains those 2 electrons to become a neutral Cu atom (this gain of electrons is reduction). Both oxidation and reduction happen simultaneously via a direct transfer of electrons from zinc to copper ions, which is exactly what defines a redox reaction.
mark_scheme: B1 experiment 2 with correct reasoning (KOH solution is the true alkali, releases OH- ions)
B1 experiment 1, with reasoning that temperature fell below the 22 °C starting value (endothermic = absorbs heat)
M1 no reaction occurs because copper is less reactive than magnesium (cannot displace it)
A1 hence no heat released/absorbed, temperature unchanged at 22 °C
M1 temperature rises faster / more steeply in experiment 5 (powder), reaching its maximum sooner (or the reverse for experiment 6)
M1 zinc powder has a larger surface area than the single piece of the same mass

A1 so more frequent collisions between zinc and Cu2+ ions / faster rate of reaction, so heat is released faster (also credit: the single piece may reach a lower maximum temperature within the five minutes)
B1 Zn loses electrons (oxidised) and Cu2+ gains electrons (reduced) simultaneously — hence redox

exam_questions.statement:
Large amounts of chemical energy are stored in the world's reserves of fossil fuels such as natural gas and petroleum (crude oil).
(a)(i) Name the main compound in natural gas. Write the word chemical equation for the complete combustion of this compound. [3]
(ii) Before it is refined, petroleum contains sulfur compounds. Describe and explain how water in rivers and lakes could become polluted if sulfur compounds are not removed from fossil fuels before they are used. [4]
(b)(i) Sulfur is removed from petroleum by combining it with hydrogen to form the gaseous compound hydrogen sulfide, H$_2$S. Complete the bonding diagram of one molecule of hydrogen sulfide to show the chemical symbols of the elements and how the outer electrons in each element are arranged. [2]
(ii) Each year, millions of tonnes of sulfur removed from petroleum are used as a raw material in the Contact Process. Name the final product of the Contact Process. [1]
exam_questions.answer:
(a)(i) Methane (CH$_4$). Word equation: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
(ii) Burning fuels containing sulfur compounds produces sulfur dioxide gas (SO$_2$). This gas dissolves in water droplets/moisture in the atmosphere, forming dilute sulfurous acid/sulfuric acid, which falls as acid rain. Acid rain that drains into rivers and lakes lowers the pH of the water (makes it more acidic), which can kill fish and other aquatic organisms directly, damage their eggs, and/or leach toxic metal ions out of surrounding rocks/soil into the water, further harming aquatic life.
(b)(i) A central sulfur atom (outer shell electron arrangement 2,6, so 6 outer electrons) shares one electron with each of two hydrogen atoms (each contributing 1 electron), forming two single covalent S–H bonds; sulfur ends with 8 electrons in its outer shell (2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs), and each hydrogen ends with 2 electrons (a full duplet).
(ii) Sulfuric acid (H$_2$SO$_4$).
exam_questions.full_solution:
Natural gas is composed mainly of methane, CH$_4$. Its complete combustion requires an excess of oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water: CH$_4$ + 2O$_2$ → CO$_2$ + 2H$_2$O (checked: C 1=1, H 4=4, O 4=4, balanced), i.e. in words: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.

If sulfur compounds in petroleum/fossil fuels are not removed before combustion, burning them converts the sulfur to sulfur dioxide (S + O$_2$ → SO$_2$). SO$_2$ is an acidic gas: it dissolves in atmospheric water vapour/cloud droplets to form sulfurous acid (H$_2$SO$_3$), which can be further oxidised to sulfuric acid (H$_2$SO$_4$); this falls to Earth as acid rain. When acid rain runs off into rivers and lakes it lowers the pH of the water, which is directly toxic to fish and other aquatic organisms (damages gills, prevents eggs hatching) and can also dissolve/leach aluminium and other metal ions out of the surrounding soil and rock into the water, adding a further toxic effect.

Hydrogen sulfide, H$_2$S: sulfur (Group 6, outer shell 2,6, needs 2 more electrons for a full octet) forms two single covalent bonds, one to each hydrogen atom (each hydrogen needs 1 more electron for a full duplet, like helium). The dot-and-cross diagram shows the S atom with 6 outer electrons (say, as dots), with each H atom's single electron (as a cross) shared in a bonding pair between S and that H — S ends up surrounded by 4 pairs of electrons (8 total: 2 shared pairs + 2 lone pairs), each H by 1 shared pair (2 electrons total).

The Contact Process converts sulfur (recovered from petroleum as above) into sulfur dioxide (burning in air), which is then catalytically oxidised (vanadium(V) oxide catalyst) to sulfur trioxide, which is finally converted to sulfuric acid (via oleum, then dilution with water): the final commercial product of the whole process is sulfuric acid, H$_2$SO$_4$.
mark_scheme: B1 methane (CH4)
B1 methane + oxygen (reactants correct)
B1 → carbon dioxide + water (products correct)
M1 SO2 formed on combustion of sulfur compounds, is an acidic gas
M1 dissolves in atmospheric water to form acid rain (sulfurous/sulfuric acid)
A1 acid rain lowers pH of rivers/lakes, harms/kills aquatic life (fish, eggs)
A1 further detail: e.g. leaches toxic metal ions from rock/soil into the water
B1 S with 6 outer electrons shown, sharing 1 electron with each of 2 H atoms (2 single covalent bonds)
B1 S has 8 outer electrons (octet) after bonding, each H has 2 (duplet)
B1 sulfuric acid

exam_questions.statement:
(a) When sodium is burned in air a mixture of solid products, which contains the ionic compound sodium oxide, is produced. Figure 7.1 shows a sodium atom (electron arrangement 2,8,1) and an oxygen atom (electron arrangement 2,6) as they exist just before sodium oxide starts to form.
(i) Describe how sodium and oxygen atoms become bonded together. Your answer should explain why the formula of sodium oxide is Na$_2$O. [3]
(ii) Describe two differences in the properties of a typical ionic compound and a typical covalent compound. [2]
(b) Figure 7.2 shows apparatus for electrolysing dilute sulfuric acid: a d.c. power supply, an ammeter, a variable resistor, and two gas-collection tubes — one (connected to the positive terminal) collecting 'gas P', the other (connected to the negative terminal) collecting hydrogen. Table 7.1 gives: experiment 1, current 0.48 A, time 400 s, volume of hydrogen collected 24 cm$^3$; experiment 2, current 0.24 A, time 400 s, volume of hydrogen collected 12 cm$^3$.
(i) Name gas P. [1]
(ii) Calculate the rate at which hydrogen was produced in experiment 1. Show your working and state the units. [2]
(iii) Calculate the number of moles of hydrogen produced in experiment 2. Assume the volume of one mole of gas under the conditions of the experiment is 24 dm$^3$. Show your working. [2]
(iv) All dilute solutions of acid contain hydrogen ions, H$^+$. Explain the difference between the results for experiments 1 and 2 in terms of electrons, ions, atoms and electric current. [3]
exam_questions.answer:
(a)(i) Sodium (2,8,1) loses its 1 outer electron to achieve a full, stable outer shell (2,8, like neon), forming a Na$^+$ ion; oxygen (2,6) needs to gain 2 electrons to achieve a full outer shell (2,8), forming an O$^{2-}$ ion. Because sodium can only donate 1 electron but oxygen needs 2, two sodium atoms are required to supply the 2 electrons needed by one oxygen atom — giving 2 Na$^+$ ions for every 1 O$^{2-}$ ion, i.e. the formula Na$_2$O. The oppositely charged ions are then held together by strong electrostatic (ionic) attraction.
(ii) e.g. (1) Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points (strong electrostatic forces throughout a giant lattice), whereas covalent (simple molecular) compounds generally have low melting and boiling points (only weak forces between molecules). (2) Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution (free-moving ions), but not as solids; simple covalent compounds do not conduct electricity in any state (no free charged particles).
(b)(i) Oxygen.
(ii) Rate = 24 cm$^3$ ÷ 400 s = 0.06 cm$^3$/s.
(iii) Moles = 12 cm$^3$ ÷ 24 000 cm$^3$/mol = 0.0005 mol (5 × 10$^{-4}$ mol).
(iv) Experiment 1 uses double the current of experiment 2 (0.48 A vs 0.24 A). Current is the rate of flow of charge (electrons) around the circuit, so a doubled current means electrons flow around the external circuit twice as fast. At the cathode (negative electrode), H$^+$ ions gain electrons (are reduced) to form H atoms, which then pair up to form H$_2$ molecules (gas); doubling the current doubles the rate at which electrons arrive at the cathode, so doubles the rate at which H$^+$ ions are discharged, which doubles the volume (and moles) of hydrogen gas produced in the same time — consistent with 24 cm$^3$ in experiment 1 vs 12 cm$^3$ in experiment 2.
exam_questions.full_solution:
Sodium's outer-shell electron arrangement is 2,8,1 — one electron away from a full outer shell. Oxygen's is 2,6 — two electrons short of a full outer shell. In forming sodium oxide, each sodium atom transfers its 1 outer electron to an oxygen atom; since oxygen needs 2 electrons but each sodium atom can only supply 1, two sodium atoms must each give up their electron to the same oxygen atom. This produces 2 Na$^+$ ions (each now with the stable 2,8 arrangement, like neon) and 1 O$^{2-}$ ion (also now 2,8), in the ratio 2:1 — hence the formula Na$_2$O. The Na$^+$ and O$^{2-}$ ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (ionic bonding) extending in all directions in a giant ionic lattice.

Typical ionic vs covalent (simple molecular) property differences arise directly from their structures: ionic compounds are giant lattices held by strong electrostatic forces acting in every direction, requiring a lot of energy to break — hence high melting/boiling points; simple covalent molecules are individual small molecules held to each other only by weak intermolecular forces (though the covalent bonds inside each molecule are strong) — hence low melting/boiling points, as only the weak forces between molecules need to be overcome. Similarly, ionic compounds contain charged ions that are free to move and carry charge once molten or dissolved (so they conduct electricity in those states, but not as a rigid solid where ions are fixed in the lattice); simple covalent compounds have no charged particles at all, so they never conduct electricity.

In the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid, H$^+$ ions migrate to the negative electrode (cathode), where they are reduced (gain an electron each) to form H atoms, which combine in pairs to form H$_2$ gas — this is the tube labelled 'hydrogen' in the diagram, connected to the negative terminal. At the positive electrode (anode), 'gas P' is produced — in dilute sulfuric acid this is oxygen, formed by the oxidation of water/hydroxide ions (sulfate ions are not easily discharged).

Rate of hydrogen production in experiment 1 = volume ÷ time = 24 cm$^3$ ÷ 400 s = 0.06 cm$^3$/s.

Moles of hydrogen in experiment 2: using n = V ÷ V$_m$ with V$_m$ = 24 dm$^3$ = 24 000 cm$^3$ per mole, n = 12 cm$^3$ ÷ 24 000 cm$^3$/mol = 5 × 10$^{-4}$ mol = 0.0005 mol.

Comparing experiments 1 and 2: the current in experiment 1 (0.48 A) is exactly double that in experiment 2 (0.24 A), for the same time (400 s). Current is the rate of flow of charge, i.e. the rate at which electrons move around the external circuit and are supplied to/removed from the electrodes. A higher current means electrons arrive at the cathode faster, so H$^+$ ions are converted to H atoms (and hence H$_2$ molecules) faster — more H$^+$ ions are discharged per second. Over the same 400 s, twice the current should discharge (approximately) twice as many H$^+$ ions and so produce twice the volume/moles of hydrogen gas — exactly what the data shows (24 cm$^3$ vs 12 cm$^3$), consistent with Faraday's laws of electrolysis (amount of substance produced at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed, i.e. to current × time).

M1 explanation that O needs 2 electrons but Na can only give 1, so 2 Na atoms are needed per O atom
A1 correct conclusion: formula is Na2O because of the 2:1 ratio of Na+ : O2- ions
B1 difference 1 (e.g. melting/boiling point): ionic high, covalent low, with reasoning (strong ionic forces throughout lattice vs weak intermolecular forces)
B1 difference 2 (e.g. electrical conductivity): ionic conducts molten/dissolved (free ions), covalent does not conduct (no free charges)
B1 oxygen
A1 = 0.06 cm3/s (units required)
M1 current is rate of flow of electrons/charge; double current means electrons flow/arrive twice as fast
M1 at cathode H+ ions gain electrons (reduced) to form H atoms then H2 gas
A1 double current discharges H+ ions twice as fast, giving twice the volume of H2 in the same time

exam_questions.statement:
Most elements in the Periodic Table can be classified as metals or non-metals. Table 8.1 lists the elements of Group 4: C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb.
(a) Use the classification of metal or non-metal to describe how the Group 4 elements differ from both Group 1 (alkali metals) and Group 7 (halogens). [2]
(b) Carbon occurs naturally in the Earth's crust as the uncombined element. Diamond and graphite are different allotropes of carbon with very different physical properties. Figure 8.1 shows a small section of the structure of one of the carbon allotropes: a layered arrangement of carbon atoms, each covalently bonded to its neighbours within a layer, with the layers stacked on top of one another. State and explain one use of the carbon allotrope shown in Figure 8.1. [2]
(c) Figure 8.2 shows apparatus used to extract lead from lead oxide, PbO, by passing hydrogen gas over heated lead oxide in a U-tube, with excess hydrogen burnt off and water condensing inside the (cooled) U-tube.
(i) Construct a balanced symbol equation for the reaction between hydrogen and lead oxide. [2]
(ii) Suggest why the method shown in Figure 8.2 could not be used to extract calcium from calcium oxide. [2]
exam_questions.answer:
(a) Group 4 elements are a mixture of non-metals at the top of the group (carbon, silicon are non-metals/metalloid-like) and metals towards the bottom (tin, lead are metals) — i.e. Group 4 contains both metals and non-metals. By contrast, Group 1 elements are all metals (alkali metals), and Group 7 elements are all non-metals (halogens).
(b) The allotrope shown is graphite (layers of hexagonally-arranged carbon atoms, each bonded to 3 neighbours, with weak forces between layers). Use: as an electrode in electrolysis (e.g. in the extraction of aluminium) — because graphite's delocalised electrons (not used in the 3 covalent bonds per carbon atom) can move freely within each layer, making it a good electrical conductor; graphite is also used as a lubricant/in pencils because the layers can slide over each other (only weak forces hold them together), making it soft and slippery.
(c)(i) H$_2$(g) + PbO(s) → Pb(s) + H$_2$O(l/g)
(ii) Calcium is more reactive than hydrogen (higher in the reactivity series), so hydrogen cannot remove oxygen from (cannot reduce) calcium oxide — only a metal above hydrogen keeps its oxide intact against reduction by hydrogen; hydrogen can only reduce the oxides of metals below it in the reactivity series (such as lead).
exam_questions.full_solution:
Looking down Group 4 (C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb), the elements change character from non-metal (carbon, silicon) through metalloid (germanium) to metal (tin, lead) — Group 4 is the group that straddles the metal/non-metal divide, containing both types of element. This contrasts with Group 1, whose members (Li, Na, K, …) are all reactive metals, and Group 7, whose members (F, Cl, Br, I) are all non-metals.

Figure 8.1's layered hexagonal structure, with carbon atoms covalently bonded to 3 neighbours within a flat layer, and weak forces holding separate layers together, is the structure of graphite (as opposed to diamond's rigid 3-D lattice where each carbon is bonded to 4 neighbours). In graphite, each carbon atom uses only 3 of its 4 outer electrons in covalent bonds, leaving one electron per atom delocalised and free to move along the layers; this gives graphite electrical conductivity (unusual for a non-metal), which is exploited by using it as inert electrodes in electrolysis. Alternatively, because the layers are only weakly held together they can easily slide over one another, making graphite soft and a good lubricant (and the basis of pencil 'lead').

For the extraction of lead: hydrogen gas passed over heated lead oxide reduces it to lead metal, while the hydrogen itself is oxidised to water: H$_2$ + PbO → Pb + H$_2$O (checked: H 2=2, Pb 1=1, O 1=1, balanced). This works because lead sits below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so hydrogen is reactive enough to strip the oxygen away from lead.

Calcium, however, sits well above hydrogen in the reactivity series (calcium is far more reactive). A less reactive element (hydrogen) cannot displace a more reactive one (calcium) from its compound — i.e. hydrogen cannot remove the oxygen from calcium oxide, so this method of reduction cannot be used to obtain calcium metal from CaO; a more powerful method is needed instead, such as electrolysis of molten calcium compounds.

A1 contrasted correctly with Group 1 (all metals) and Group 7 (all non-metals)
B1 identifies graphite as the allotrope shown
M1 valid use stated (e.g. electrode / lubricant / pencils) with correct structural reasoning (delocalised electrons conduct, or weak forces between layers let them slide)
M1 H2 + PbO -> Pb + H2O reactants/products correct
A1 equation balanced
M1 calcium is more reactive than hydrogen (higher in reactivity series)
A1 so hydrogen cannot reduce calcium oxide / cannot remove oxygen from it

exam_questions.statement:
(a) Dutch metal is an alloy of copper and zinc formed into very thin sheets. When a small piece of Dutch metal is dropped into a container filled with chlorine gas, it bursts into flame and two compounds are produced (Figure 9.1).
(i) State the meaning of the term alloy. [1]
(ii) State the physical property of metals that allows them to be formed into very thin sheets. [1]
(iii) Suggest the names of the two compounds formed when Dutch metal reacts with chlorine. [1]
(b) Sodium burns in oxygen gas to produce a white solid containing the ionic compound sodium oxide. Figure 9.2 shows a sodium atom (electron arrangement 2,8,1) and an oxygen atom (electron arrangement 2,6). Predict and explain, in terms of changes in electronic structure, the chemical formula of sodium oxide. [3]
(c) Phosphorus is a non-metallic element containing molecules with formula P$_4$. The chemical formula of phosphorus oxide shows four phosphorus atoms bonded with ten oxygen atoms. Construct a balanced symbolic equation for the reaction between phosphorus and oxygen gas to form phosphorus oxide. [3]
exam_questions.answer:
(a)(i) An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually another metal, or sometimes carbon).
(ii) Malleability (metals can be hammered/rolled into thin sheets).
(iii) Copper(II) chloride and zinc chloride.
(b) Sodium (2,8,1) loses its single outer electron to form a stable Na$^+$ ion (electron arrangement 2,8, like neon); oxygen (2,6) gains 2 electrons to form a stable O$^{2-}$ ion (electron arrangement 2,8). Since each sodium atom can only donate 1 electron but each oxygen atom needs 2, two sodium atoms are needed to supply the electrons for each oxygen atom, giving the formula Na$_2$O.
(c) P$_4$ + 5O$_2$ → P$_4$O$_{10}$
exam_questions.full_solution:
An alloy is formed by mixing a metal with one or more other elements (commonly another metal, sometimes a non-metal like carbon) while molten, which then solidifies as a new material with different (usually more useful, e.g. harder or more corrosion-resistant) properties than the pure metal alone. Dutch metal is an alloy of copper and zinc.

Metals can be beaten into thin sheets because they are malleable: in the giant metallic lattice, layers of positive metal ions can slide over one another under force without breaking the metallic bonding (the sea of delocalised electrons re-forms around the ions in their new positions), unlike brittle ionic/covalent solids which shatter when struck.

Since Dutch metal contains both copper and zinc, and chlorine reacts with reactive metals to form metal chlorides, the two products are copper(II) chloride (CuCl$_2$) and zinc chloride (ZnCl$_2$).

Formation of sodium oxide: sodium's outer electron arrangement 2,8,1 is one electron more than the stable noble-gas arrangement 2,8, so it readily loses that 1 electron to form Na$^+$. Oxygen's arrangement 2,6 is 2 electrons short of the stable arrangement 2,8, so it gains 2 electrons to form O$^{2-}$. Because 1 sodium atom can only supply 1 electron, but 1 oxygen atom requires 2, two sodium atoms must each donate their single electron to the same oxygen atom; this gives 2 Na$^+$ ions for every O$^{2-}$ ion, i.e. the formula Na$_2$O, with the ions held together by strong electrostatic (ionic) attraction.

For phosphorus oxide: phosphorus exists as P$_4$ molecules, and we are told the oxide's formula contains 4 P atoms bonded to 10 O atoms, i.e. P$_4$O$_{10}$. Since oxygen gas is diatomic (O$_2$), balancing the oxygen atoms (10 needed, 2 per O$_2$ molecule) requires 5 O$_2$ molecules: P$_4$ + 5O$_2$ → P$_4$O$_{10}$. Checking: P atoms, 4 = 4; O atoms, 5×2 = 10 = 10 — balanced.
mark_scheme: B1 alloy = a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements
B1 malleability / metals can be hammered or rolled into shape
B1 copper(II) chloride and zinc chloride (both needed)
M1 Na (2,8,1) loses 1 electron to become Na+ (2,8); O (2,6) gains 2 electrons to become O2- (2,8)
M1 reasoning that 2 Na atoms are needed to supply the 2 electrons required by 1 O atom
A1 correct formula Na2O stated/justified
M1 correct reactants and product P4 + ?O2 -> P4O10 set up
A1 balanced with coefficient 5 in front of O2
B1 equation fully balanced and checked (P: 4=4, O: 10=10)

exam_questions.statement:
**Extension (molar concentration is beyond the 0654 syllabus).** (a) A colourless gas contained in a flask is either propane or propene.
(i) The gas is shaken with bromine solution. Describe the observation, if any, that would be made if the gas is: propane; propene. [2]
(ii) Describe one difference between the structures of propane and propene molecules. [1]
(b) Ethanol, C$_2$H$_6$O, is produced from glucose, C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$, in a fermentation reaction: C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$(aq) → 2C$_2$H$_6$O(aq) + 2CO$_2$(g). The reaction starts when yeast is added to the aqueous glucose solution; the gas produced is bubbled through limewater (Figure 10.1).
(i) Describe how and explain why the appearance of the limewater changes during the fermentation reaction. [2]
(ii) Calculate the relative molecular mass of glucose, C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$. Show your working. [1]
(iii) Calculate the mass of glucose that has to be dissolved in 5.0 dm$^3$ of water to produce a solution whose concentration is 3.5 mol/dm$^3$. Show your working. [2]
(c)(i) Name the element present in all amino acids but not in ethanol. [1]
(ii) Many different amino acids exist in nature. Name the compound formed when amino acids link together in a condensation polymerisation reaction. [1]
exam_questions.answer:
(a)(i) Propane: no visible change — the orange/brown bromine colour stays (no reaction). Propene: the orange/brown bromine colour is decolorised/turns colourless (an addition reaction occurs across the double bond, forming 1,2-dibromopropane).
(ii) Propane contains only single (C–C) bonds (it is saturated); propene contains one carbon–carbon double bond, C=C (it is unsaturated).
(b)(i) The limewater turns cloudy/milky, because the carbon dioxide gas produced in fermentation reacts with the calcium hydroxide in limewater to form an insoluble white precipitate of calcium carbonate.
(ii) Relative molecular mass = (6×12) + (12×1) + (6×16) = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180.
(iii) Moles of glucose needed = 3.5 mol/dm$^3$ × 5.0 dm$^3$ = 17.5 mol. Mass = 17.5 mol × 180 g/mol = 3150 g.
(c)(i) Nitrogen.
(ii) Protein.
exam_questions.full_solution:
Bromine water/solution is the standard test for carbon–carbon double bonds (unsaturation). Propane (C$_3$H$_8$) is a saturated alkane with only single bonds, so there is nothing for bromine to add across — the solution stays its original orange/brown colour (no reaction). Propene (C$_3$H$_6$) contains one C=C double bond, so bromine molecules add across the double bond (an addition reaction, forming 1,2-dibromopropane), decolorising the bromine from orange/brown to colourless. The structural difference asked for in (ii) is that a propene molecule has a C=C double bond, whereas a propane molecule has only single bonds.

During fermentation (yeast enzymes converting glucose to ethanol and CO$_2$), the CO$_2$ gas produced is passed through limewater (a solution of calcium hydroxide). CO$_2$ reacts with calcium hydroxide: Ca(OH)$_2$(aq) + CO$_2$(g) → CaCO$_3$(s) + H$_2$O(l). Calcium carbonate is insoluble in water, so it appears as a fine white precipitate suspended through the liquid, turning the limewater cloudy/milky — this is the standard test confirming CO$_2$ gas is present.

Relative molecular mass of glucose, C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$: using A$_r$(C)=12, A$_r$(H)=1, A$_r$(O)=16, M$_r$ = 6(12) + 12(1) + 6(16) = 72 + 12 + 96 = 180 (verified by direct arithmetic).

To make a 3.5 mol/dm$^3$ solution in 5.0 dm$^3$ of water: moles required = concentration × volume = 3.5 × 5.0 = 17.5 mol. Converting moles to mass using mass = moles × M$_r$: mass = 17.5 × 180 = 3150 g (verified by direct multiplication).

Amino acids all contain an amine group (–NH$_2$) as well as a carboxylic acid group (–COOH) and an R group; the amine group is the source of nitrogen in every amino acid. Ethanol (C$_2$H$_6$O) contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen — no nitrogen — so nitrogen is the element present in amino acids but absent from ethanol. When many amino acid molecules join together by condensation polymerisation (forming peptide bonds, releasing a water molecule at each new bond), the resulting long-chain polymer is called a protein.
mark_scheme: B1 propane: no change (bromine stays orange/brown)
B1 propene: bromine decolorised/turns colourless
B1 propane has only single (C-C) bonds / propene has a C=C double bond (saturated vs unsaturated)
M1 limewater turns cloudy/milky
A1 because CO2 reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate
B1 Mr = 180, with working shown (6x12 + 12x1 + 6x16)
M1 moles = 3.5 x 5.0 = 17.5 mol
B1 nitrogen
B1 protein

exam_questions.statement:
(a) In the Periodic Table the elements are organised into groups and periods.
(i) State the total number of elements in the period that includes nitrogen, N. [1]
(ii) Figure 11.1 shows the electron arrangement (2,5) and the number of protons (7) in one atom of nitrogen. Name the other type of sub-atomic particle contained in this nucleus. [1]
(iii) Draw a diagram, similar to Figure 11.1, to show an atom of the element phosphorus, P (proton number 15). [2]
(b) Hydrogen, proton number 1, combines with nitrogen to produce the covalent compound ammonia, NH$_3$. Complete the covalent bonding diagram of one molecule of ammonia, showing the chemical symbols of each atom and how the outer electrons of each atom are arranged. [2]
(c) Ammonia is made industrially by reacting nitrogen and hydrogen together on the surface of a solid material containing iron (Figure 11.2).
(i) State the name of the industrial process shown in Figure 11.2. [1]
(ii) Hydrogen gas for the process is produced by reacting methane, CH$_4$, with steam, H$_2$O. In this reaction each methane reacts with one molecule of steam, producing three molecules of hydrogen. Deduce the balanced symbol equation for this reaction. [3]
(iii) State the purpose of the solid material containing iron used in the process shown in Figure 11.2. [1]
exam_questions.answer:
(a)(i) Nitrogen is in Period 2, which contains 8 elements (Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Ne).
(ii) Neutrons.
(iii) Phosphorus (proton number 15) has electron arrangement 2,8,5: a nucleus (labelled '15 protons') surrounded by three electron shells containing 2, 8 and 5 electrons respectively (drawn as concentric circles with the correct number of electrons marked on each).
(b) A central N atom (outer-shell arrangement 2,5) shares one electron with each of three H atoms (each contributing 1 electron), forming three single covalent N–H bonds; nitrogen ends up with 8 outer electrons (3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair), and each hydrogen ends up with 2 electrons (full duplet).
(c)(i) The Haber process (Haber–Bosch process).
(ii) CH$_4$ + H$_2$O → CO + 3H$_2$
(iii) It acts as a catalyst: it speeds up the rate of the reaction (so ammonia is produced faster) without being used up/consumed itself.
exam_questions.full_solution:
Nitrogen (proton number 7) is in Period 2 of the Periodic Table, which runs from lithium (3) to neon (10) — counting Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Ne gives 8 elements in this period.

An atom's nucleus contains protons and neutrons (electrons orbit outside the nucleus in shells); since the 7 protons are already specified for nitrogen, the other particle present in the nucleus is the neutron.

Phosphorus has proton (atomic) number 15, so a neutral atom has 15 electrons, filling shells in the pattern 2, 8, 5 (first shell holds up to 2, second up to 8, and the remaining 5 go into the third shell) — this mirrors Figure 11.1's style, but with 15 protons in the nucleus and three concentric shells containing 2, 8 and 5 electrons respectively.

In ammonia, NH$_3$: nitrogen's outer shell (2,5) needs 3 more electrons for a stable octet; each hydrogen atom (1 electron) needs 1 more for a stable duplet. Nitrogen shares one electron with each of 3 separate hydrogen atoms, forming 3 covalent N–H bonds. After bonding, nitrogen has 8 outer electrons (3 shared pairs plus 1 lone, unshared pair), and each hydrogen has 2 (its own electron plus nitrogen's shared one).

The industrial synthesis of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen over an iron-containing catalyst is the Haber process (sometimes called the Haber–Bosch process).

For the methane + steam reaction: we are told 1 molecule of methane reacts with 1 molecule of steam to give 3 molecules of hydrogen, with carbon ending up in a product too (steam reforming produces carbon monoxide): CH$_4$ + H$_2$O → CO + 3H$_2$. Checking atoms: left-hand side C=1, H=4+2=6, O=1; right-hand side C=1 (in CO), O=1 (in CO), H=3×2=6 (in 3H$_2$) — all balance (1=1 C, 6=6 H, 1=1 O), confirming the equation as given is correctly balanced with these exact (1,1,1,3) coefficients.

The solid material containing iron in the Haber process is a catalyst: it provides a surface on which nitrogen and hydrogen molecules can more easily break their strong bonds and react, lowering the activation energy and so increasing the rate at which the reaction reaches equilibrium — the iron itself is not used up and does not change the position of the equilibrium (the percentage yield of ammonia), only how quickly it is reached.

B1 neutrons
B1 correct number of electrons per shell (2,8,5) shown
B1 correct nucleus label (15 protons) and 3 shells drawn clearly
B1 N shares 1 electron with each of 3 H atoms, 3 single covalent bonds shown
B1 N ends with 8 outer electrons (octet, incl. 1 lone pair), each H with 2 (duplet)
B1 Haber process (accept Haber-Bosch process)
M1 correct unbalanced skeleton CH4 + H2O -> CO + H2 identified as the reaction type
M1 coefficient 3 placed in front of H2 (as given: 3 molecules of hydrogen produced)
A1 equation balanced and checked: CH4 + H2O -> CO + 3H2 (C:1=1, H:6=6, O:1=1)
B1 acts as a catalyst / speeds up the reaction without being used up

exam_questions.statement:
Salts are produced when acids are neutralised.
(a) Using only substances chosen from the list (hydrochloric acid, hydrogen, magnesium, magnesium carbonate, magnesium oxide, sulfuric acid, water, zinc, zinc carbonate, zinc oxide — each substance may be used once, more than once, or not at all), complete the word equations for the reactions that produce the two salts, magnesium sulfate and zinc sulfate:
____ + ____ → magnesium sulfate + hydrogen
____ + ____ → zinc sulfate + carbon dioxide + ____ [2]
(b) Figure 12.1 shows the temperature change when sodium hydrogencarbonate solution reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid: temperature of reactants = 25 °C, temperature of products = 21 °C.
(i) Complete the equation to show the type of energy transformation that occurs in this reaction: ____ energy → ____ energy. [1]
(ii) Explain your answer to (b)(i). [1]
(c) Figure 12.2 shows apparatus (side-arm test-tube in a controlled-temperature water-bath, connected to a gas syringe) a student uses to investigate the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and excess dilute hydrochloric acid. The student pushes the piston fully in, adds a known amount of acid and checks the temperature is steady, adds a known mass of calcium carbonate, places the bung and starts the stopwatch, and records the volume of gas in the syringe every 10 seconds for 90 seconds. Figure 12.3 shows a graph of volume/cm$^3$ against time/seconds, rising steeply at first then levelling off to a plateau at roughly 90–95 cm$^3$ by about 60–70 seconds, remaining flat from 75 s to 90 s.
(i) Explain the shape of the graph between 75 and 90 seconds. [2]
(ii) The student repeats the experiment using half the mass of calcium carbonate, keeping all other variables the same. Sketch (describe) the graph of the results from this second experiment. [3]
(iii) Explain, in terms of collisions, why the rate of the reaction increases when the temperature of the acid is increased. [2]
exam_questions.answer:
(a) magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + hydrogen
zinc carbonate + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + carbon dioxide + water
(b)(i) thermal (heat) energy → chemical energy (the energy transfer runs from the surroundings into the reacting chemicals).
(ii) Since the temperature of the reaction mixture fell (25 °C → 21 °C), the reaction took in thermal energy from its surroundings and stored it as chemical energy in the products — i.e. it is an endothermic reaction, so the direction of energy transfer is from the surroundings (heat) to the chemicals (as stored chemical energy).
(c)(i) The graph is flat/horizontal between 75 s and 90 s because the reaction has finished — all of the calcium carbonate (the limiting reactant, since the hydrochloric acid is in excess) has been used up, so no more gas (CO$_2$) can be produced; the volume of gas in the syringe therefore stays constant.
(ii) The new curve would start at the origin, lie below the first curve and level off (become horizontal) at about half the final volume of the first experiment (roughly 45–48 cm$^3$ instead of about 93 cm$^3$), because only half the mass (moles) of calcium carbonate, the limiting reactant, is available to produce carbon dioxide. Its initial gradient should be no steeper than the first curve: with half the mass of calcium carbonate there is less surface area for the acid to react with, so the initial rate is likely to be lower.
(iii) Increasing the temperature gives the reacting particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more frequently; more importantly, a greater proportion of these collisions now have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy, so a greater fraction of collisions are successful (lead to a reaction), which increases the rate of reaction.
exam_questions.full_solution:
(a) Matching the word bank to the standard reaction patterns: a reactive metal + an acid → a salt + hydrogen gives magnesium + sulfuric acid → magnesium sulfate + hydrogen (checked: Mg + H$_2$SO$_4$ → MgSO$_4$ + H$_2$, atoms balance: Mg 1=1, H 2=2, S 1=1, O 4=4). A metal carbonate + an acid → a salt + carbon dioxide + water gives zinc carbonate + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + carbon dioxide + water (checked: ZnCO$_3$ + H$_2$SO$_4$ → ZnSO$_4$ + CO$_2$ + H$_2$O, atoms balance: Zn 1=1, C 1=1, O 7=7, H 2=2, S 1=1).

(b) The temperature falling below the starting value (25 °C down to 21 °C) is the signature of an endothermic reaction: heat energy is taken in from the surroundings (cooling them) and converted into chemical (potential) energy stored within the products, i.e. the energy transformation is thermal energy → chemical energy.

(c)(i) The flat section of the graph (75–90 s) indicates no further gas is being produced. Since hydrochloric acid is stated to be in excess, the calcium carbonate is the limiting reactant — once it is completely consumed the reaction stops (regardless of how much acid remains), so the syringe reading plateaus at a fixed maximum volume.

(c)(ii) Halving the mass of calcium carbonate halves the total amount (moles) of this limiting reactant available, so the total volume of CO$_2$ that can ever be produced is also approximately halved (roughly 45–48 cm$^3$ instead of ~90–95 cm$^3$, since gas volume produced is proportional to moles of CaCO$_3$ reacted). The acid concentration is the same, but the calcium carbonate is the limiting reactant and there is only half as much of it, so there is less surface area of solid for the acid to react with: the initial rate is likely to be lower, and the curve should be no steeper than the original at the start and lie below it throughout. It still levels off (becomes horizontal) within the 90 seconds, at about half the original final volume.

(c)(iii) Collision theory: for a reaction to occur, particles must collide with each other with at least the minimum energy required (the activation energy). Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the particles, so they move faster; this has two effects — more frequent collisions overall, but, crucially, a much larger proportion of those collisions now have energy ≥ the activation energy (the energy distribution of particle speeds shifts so that far more particles exceed the activation-energy threshold). It is this big increase in the proportion of successful (effective) collisions, not just the modest increase in collision frequency, that is mainly responsible for the large increase in reaction rate with temperature.
